Adult female Tilefish (Lopholatilus villarii) have been documented to attain a remarkable ultimate fork length of 107 centimeters [Li = 107 centimeters], a size that positions them among the larger members of the family Malacanthidae. This maximum recorded dimension was derived from a long-term trawl survey conducted along the continental shelf off southern Brazil, where specimens exceeding one meter in fork length are infrequently captured. The planktivorous feeding habits of this species likely support such substantial somatic growth, as they exploit dense aggregations of gelatinous zooplankton and small pelagic crustaceans. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the attainment of such a large body size is accompanied by a correspondingly extended period of somatic development. In females, the fork length at puberty has been estimated at 34 centimeters [Lp = 34 centimeters], indicating that reproductive maturation begins relatively early in the lifespan relative to the ultimate adult size. This value was established through histological examination of ovarian tissue from a size-stratified sample of individuals collected during the austral summer spawning season. The onset of gonadal activity at this moderate fork length suggests a life-history strategy that balances early reproductive investment with continued somatic growth toward the asymptotic length.

The wet weight at birth for newly hatched Tilefish larvae is approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of 0.85 millimeters recorded for the closely related lutjanid species Lutjanus stellatus and converted using the standard spherical volume formula for a teleost egg. This remarkably small initial mass places the yolk-sac larva firmly within the lecithotrophic phase, during which the prolarva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. Upon eclosion, the chorionate embryo undergoes a brief period of rapid yolk absorption, with the mouth not yet fully developed in the earliest alevin stage. The low birth weight reflects the energetic constraints of producing large numbers of small pelagic eggs, a common reproductive strategy among demersal spawning marine fishes. Comparative studies within the Malacanthidae indicate that such a small larval size is associated with a high dispersal potential during the planktonic phase, which may facilitate gene flow across the species' relatively broad geographic range along the southwestern Atlantic margin. The transition to the exotrophic larval stage occurs once the yolk reserves are fully depleted.

Under stable thermal conditions maintained at 14.7 °C [T = 14.7 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of Tilefish has been estimated based on data derived from the congener Lopholatilus chamaeleonticeps, which exhibits a closely comparable spawning strategy. This rate corresponds to approximately 21,918 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 21,918 eggs per day] across an extended spawning season, with each gravid individual releasing multiple batches of pelagic eggs over the course of several months. In practice, spawning events are discrete and separated by intervals of ovarian recrudescence, so the daily rate is a composite measure of continuous propagule production. This high-frequency, low-fecundity-per-event pattern is adaptive for a species that releases buoyant eggs into a variable pelagic environment, where high mortality during the early larval stages selects for sustained reproductive output over an extended breeding season.

Longevity estimates for Tilefish, derived from otolith-based age validation studies conducted at a water temperature of 14.7 °C [T = 14.7 °C], indicate that the maximum lifespan spans approximately 12,775 days [am = approximately 12,775 days], which corresponds to roughly 35 years. This considerable lifespan is among the highest recorded for temperate demersal fishes in the southwestern Atlantic and suggests a slow-paced life-history strategy characterized by delayed senescence. The extended longevity is likely facilitated by the species' occupation of a relatively stable thermal niche within the outer continental shelf, where seasonal temperature fluctuations are modest and food resources are consistently available year-round. From a demographic perspective, such a long lifespan buffers the population against occasional recruitment failures, as older, reproductively experienced individuals can continue contributing to annual spawning biomass across multiple decades. Comparative age data from the Gulf of Mexico population of Lopholatilus chamaeleonticeps show a similar longevity pattern, reinforcing the hypothesis that the genus as a whole has evolved an extended lifespan in response to the predictable but moderately productive benthic environments it inhabits.

The time since birth at puberty for female Tilefish, determined at the same thermal regime of 14.7 °C [T = 14.7 °C], is approximately 2,190 days [tp = approximately 2,190 days], which equates to roughly six years based on the 5-7 year range reported in the literature from gonadal staging studies. This relatively protracted pre-reproductive period is consistent with the species' large ultimate body size and extended lifespan; many large-bodied, slow-growing marine fishes delay sexual maturation until a substantial portion of somatic growth is completed. The onset of vitellogenesis and the first signs of ovarian maturation are typically observed in individuals that have recently transitioned from the juvenile to the sub-adult stage, marked by an allometric shift in body proportions and the completion of fin ray ossification. Delaying puberty until approximately six years post-hatching allows Tilefish to accumulate sufficient lipid reserves to support the high energetic demands of multiple spawning events per season. This life-history trade-off between early reproduction and continued somatic growth is a defining characteristic of the species' evolutionary strategy within the productive yet competitive demersal fish assemblage of the Brazilian continental margin.
